step.detail:
Question: What does this page say about how to bring a clinical negligence claim, who NHS Resolution deals with, whether there is a no-fault or redress scheme, and any starting points or time limits mentioned? Quote exact wording and links worth following.
The page says that to bring a clinical negligence claim you need to show both a breach of duty of care and causation, and if you do not have legal representation you should send a ‘letter of claim’ to the responsible NHS Trust. It says NHS Resolution handles claims for clinical negligence compensation, and it does not mention any no-fault or redress scheme on this page. The starting point it gives is that you may wish to use the NHS complaints procedure first, and it says personal injury claims are subject to a three-year limitation period, with no limitation period for people who lack capacity.
✓ quote found in the page: "To receive compensation, you will need to show both ‘breach of duty of care’ and ‘causation’ has taken place."
✓ quote found in the page: "If you do not have legal representation and you plan on representing yourself in court as a litigant in person, you will need to submit what is called a ‘letter of claim’ to the NHS Trust that was responsible for your care."
✓ quote found in the page: "Before making a claim it is worth considering using the NHS complaints procedure in order to find out more about what happened."
✓ quote found in the page: "Compensation claims for personal injury are subject to a ‘limitation period’ of three years."

step.detail:
Question: What does this official legislation note say about the cap on success fees in personal injury claims and what damages the cap applies to? Quote exact wording.
The note says that in a claim for personal injuries, the success fee is capped at 25% of certain damages. The cap applies to "the damages awarded for pain, suffering and loss of amenity and pecuniary loss, other than future pecuniary loss and net of any sums recoverable by the Compensation Recovery Unit, inclusive of VAT."
✓ quote found in the page: "Article 5 provides that, in a claim for personal injuries, the success fee shall be limited to a maximum of 25% of the damages awarded for pain, suffering and loss of amenity and pecuniary loss, other than future pecuniary loss and net of any sums recoverable by the Compensation Recovery Unit, inclusive of VAT."
✓ quote found in the page: "Article 5 further limits the effect of the 25% cap to proceedings at first instance."
✓ quote found in the page: "the maximum success fee which may be recovered from damages awarded for pain, suffering and loss of amenity and pecuniary loss, other than future pecuniary loss and net of any sums recoverable by the Compensation Recovery Unit, shall be a maximum of 100% of those damages, inclusive of VAT."

Question: What does this official page say about how the Ombudsman deals with complaints, including any stages, checks, or likely timeframes if mentioned? Quote exact wording and links worth following.
The page says the Ombudsman uses “a three-step process for dealing with complaints,” with Step 1 checking whether it can look into the complaint, Step 2 deciding whether to investigate, and Step 3 investigating if needed. It says Step 1 should be completed “within five working days,” and for Step 2 it considers factors like severity, whether something may have gone wrong, whether you complained within 12 months, and whether legal action was an option. If it investigates, the investigation has “five stages,” and “Every complaint is different so the time it takes will vary.”

Question: What does this official legislation page say about when clinical negligence services are in scope for civil legal aid? Quote exact wording that shows the rule and any limits.
Clinical negligence services are in scope for civil legal aid only for a claim for damages for clinical negligence that caused a neurological injury to an individual who is severely disabled, and only where both conditions are met. The page says the negligence must have occurred either while V was in the mother's womb or within the specified 8-week period after birth, and the services must be provided to V or, if V has died, to V's personal representative. The provision is also subject to listed exclusions.
✓ quote found in the page: "“Civil legal services provided in relation to a claim for damages in respect of clinical negligence which caused a neurological injury to an individual (“V”) as a result of which V is severely disabled, but only where the first and second conditions are met.”"
✓ quote found in the page: "“The first condition is that the clinical negligence occurred—”"
✓ quote found in the page: "“while V was in his or her mother's womb, or”"
✓ quote found in the page: "“The second condition is that— (a) the services are provided to V, or (b) V has died and the services are provided to V's personal representative.”"

Question: What does regulation 13 say about acknowledging a complaint and discussing how it will be handled and the response period? Quote the exact wording.
Regulation 13 says that when it acknowledges the complaint, the responsible body must offer to discuss how it will be handled and the response period. The exact wording is: “At the time it acknowledges the complaint, the responsible body must offer to discuss with the complainant, at a time to be agreed with the complainant— (a) the manner in which the complaint is to be handled; and (b) the period (“the response period”) within which— (i) the investigation of the complaint is likely to be completed; and (ii) the response required by regulation 14(2) is likely to be sent to the complainant.”

step.detail:
Question: What does regulation 14 say about investigating a complaint and sending the response? Quote the exact wording, especially anything about times or explanations.
Regulation 14 says the responsible body must investigate the complaint "in a manner appropriate to resolve it speedily and efficiently" and keep the complainant informed "as far as reasonably practicable, as to the progress of the investigation." It must then send a written response "as soon as reasonably practicable after completing the investigation," and if it is late, it must "notify the complainant in writing accordingly and explain the reason why" and send the response "as soon as reasonably practicable after the relevant period."

Question: What does this official page say about the Clinical Negligence Scheme for Trusts, who is a member, and how it relates to clinical negligence claims? Quote exact wording.
The page says the Clinical Negligence Scheme for Trusts (CNST) "handles all clinical negligence claims against member NHS bodies" for incidents on or after 1 April 1995 (or when the body joined the scheme, if later). It says membership is voluntary, but "all NHS Trusts (including Foundation Trusts) in England currently belong to the scheme." It also says that when a claim is made against a member, "the NHS body remains the legal defendant" while NHS Resolution takes over handling the claim and associated costs.

For hospital care, you can complain to the provider directly or to the commissioner, but not both.

sources.quote: Information supplied by Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust

Contact your local integrated care board (ICB) for complaints about primary care services (GPs, dentists, opticians or pharmacists) and secondary care, such as hospital care, mental health services, out-of-hours services, NHS 111 and community services like district nursing.

You can either complain to the NHS service provider directly (such as a GP, dentist surgery or hospital) or to the commissioner of the services, which is the body that pays for the NHS services you use. You cannot complain to both.
Complaints should normally be made within 12 months of an incident or of it coming to your attention.
At the time it acknowledges the complaint, the responsible body must offer to discuss with the complainant, at a time to be agreed with the complainant—
As soon as reasonably practicable after completing the investigation, the responsible body must send the complainant in writing a response, signed by the responsible person, which includes—

steps.body: Public Service Ombudsman (formerly Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman)
steps.what: If you are still unhappy after complaining to Guy's and St Thomas' or the commissioner first, the independent escalation route is the Public Service Ombudsman for NHS complaints in England. You start with its complaint checker, which leads into the online complaint form.
steps.deadline: "If you're still unhappy, complain to us within 12 months of knowing about the issue"
points: You must complain to the organisation first.
The Ombudsman says to complain to it within 12 months of knowing about the issue.
Its checker first asks what your complaint is about, including 'The NHS in England'.
Its investigation stage has five stages, but it says the overall time varies by case.
requires: A complaint to the organisation first.
steps.appliesIf: You have already complained about NHS care in England and remain unhappy with the answer or handling.
alternatives: Court claim for compensation if seeking damages for negligence.
Complaint to the Care Quality Commission is not the compensation route for an individual negligence case.
missing: Whether the trust has issued its final response yet.

steps.body: NHS Resolution / Clinical Negligence Scheme for Trusts / courts of England and Wales
steps.what: For harm from NHS care at St Thomas' Hospital, compensation is by a clinical negligence claim, usually settled or litigated under the courts of England and Wales, not by a no-fault scheme. Guy's and St Thomas' remains the legal defendant, but NHS Resolution handles the claim and pays the associated costs through the Clinical Negligence Scheme for Trusts because all NHS Trusts and Foundation Trusts in England belong to it.
steps.deadline: "Compensation claims for personal injury are subject to a ‘limitation period’ of three years."
points: To get compensation, the claimant must prove both breach of duty and causation.
If acting without a lawyer, NHS Resolution says to send a 'letter of claim' to the NHS Trust responsible for the care.
Personal injury clinical negligence claims are subject to a three-year limitation period.
All NHS Trusts, including Foundation Trusts, in England currently belong to CNST.
When a claim is made, the NHS body remains the legal defendant but NHS Resolution handles the claim and meets the associated costs.
NHS Resolution also uses mediation and other dispute resolution methods to avoid unnecessary court proceedings where possible.
steps.appliesIf: You seek money for harm caused by allegedly negligent NHS treatment at St Thomas' Hospital.
alternatives: NHS complaints procedure to get explanations before or alongside considering a claim.
Mediation or other NHS Resolution dispute resolution methods during a claim.
missing: Exact date of knowledge for limitation purposes if argued later.
Whether any limitation exception could apply, such as lack of capacity.

sources.quote: To receive compensation, you will need to show both ‘breach of duty of care’ and ‘causation’ has taken place.

If you do not have legal representation and you plan on representing yourself in court as a litigant in person, you will need to submit what is called a ‘letter of claim’ to the NHS Trust that was responsible for your care.
Compensation claims for personal injury are subject to a ‘limitation period’ of three years.
Although membership of the scheme is voluntary, all NHS Trusts (including Foundation Trusts) in England currently belong to the scheme.
When a claim is made against a member of CNST, the NHS body remains the legal defendant.
However, we take over full responsibility for handling the claim and meeting the associated costs.

sources.quote: Information supplied by Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust

Contact your local integrated care board (ICB) for complaints about primary care services (GPs, dentists, opticians or pharmacists) and secondary care, such as hospital care, mental health services, out-of-hours services, NHS 111 and community services like district nursing.

You can either complain to the NHS service provider directly (such as a GP, dentist surgery or hospital) or to the commissioner of the services, which is the body that pays for the NHS services you use. You cannot complain to both.
Complaints should normally be made within 12 months of an incident or of it coming to your attention.

requires: A complaint to the organisation first.

You can either complain to the NHS service provider directly (such as a GP, dentist surgery or hospital) or to the commissioner of the services, which is the body that pays for the NHS services you use. You cannot complain to both.
Complaints should normally be made within 12 months of an incident or of it coming to your attention.
At the time it acknowledges the complaint, the responsible body must offer to discuss with the complainant, at a time to be agreed with the complainant—
As soon as reasonably practicable after completing the investigation, the responsible body must send the complainant in writing a response, signed by the responsible person, which includes—

steps.body: Public Service Ombudsman (formerly Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman)
steps.what: If you are still unhappy after complaining to Guy's and St Thomas' or the commissioner first, the independent escalation route is the Public Service Ombudsman for NHS complaints in England. You start with its complaint checker, which leads into the online complaint form.
steps.deadline: "If you're still unhappy, complain to us within 12 months of knowing about the issue"
points: You must complain to the organisation first.
The Ombudsman says to complain to it within 12 months of knowing about the issue.
Its checker first asks what your complaint is about, including 'The NHS in England'.
Its investigation stage has five stages, but it says the overall time varies by case.
requires: A complaint to the organisation first.
steps.appliesIf: You have already complained about NHS care in England and remain unhappy with the answer or handling.
alternatives: Court claim for compensation if seeking damages for negligence.
Complaint to the Care Quality Commission is not the compensation route for an individual negligence case.
missing: Whether the trust has issued its final response yet.

sources.quote: Complain to the organisation you're unhappy with first
If you're still unhappy, complain to us within 12 months of knowing about the issue
If your complaint is ready, the checker will take you to our online complaint form.
To start with, please tell us what is your complaint about?
We have a three-step process for dealing with complaints.
We aim to complete this step within five working days of getting your complaint.

steps.body: NHS Resolution / Clinical Negligence Scheme for Trusts / courts of England and Wales
steps.what: For harm from NHS care at St Thomas' Hospital, compensation is by a clinical negligence claim, usually settled or litigated under the courts of England and Wales, not by a no-fault scheme. Guy's and St Thomas' remains the legal defendant, but NHS Resolution handles the claim and pays the associated costs through the Clinical Negligence Scheme for Trusts because all NHS Trusts and Foundation Trusts in England belong to it.
steps.deadline: "Compensation claims for personal injury are subject to a ‘limitation period’ of three years."
points: To get compensation, the claimant must prove both breach of duty and causation.
If acting without a lawyer, NHS Resolution says to send a 'letter of claim' to the NHS Trust responsible for the care.
Personal injury clinical negligence claims are subject to a three-year limitation period.
All NHS Trusts, including Foundation Trusts, in England currently belong to CNST.
When a claim is made, the NHS body remains the legal defendant but NHS Resolution handles the claim and meets the associated costs.
NHS Resolution also uses mediation and other dispute resolution methods to avoid unnecessary court proceedings where possible.
steps.appliesIf: You seek money for harm caused by allegedly negligent NHS treatment at St Thomas' Hospital.
alternatives: NHS complaints procedure to get explanations before or alongside considering a claim.
Mediation or other NHS Resolution dispute resolution methods during a claim.

steps.what: For an adult clinical negligence claim like this in England, ordinary civil legal aid is generally not available. The main funding route is usually a conditional fee agreement ('no win, no fee'); for personal injury claims, the success fee taken from damages is capped by law.

steps.body: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
steps.what: The national body that publishes the core health and care guidance used by NHS services in England is NICE. Its guidance is not a hospital complaint route, but it is the main official source to check the clinical guidance doctors are expected to use alongside specialist and local guidance.
points: NICE says it produces guidance for the NHS and wider health and care system.
Its guidance includes clinical guidelines and other evidence-based product types.
steps.appliesIf: Clinical guidance question for NHS care in England.

sources.quote: We produce useful and usable guidance for the NHS and wider health and care system.

Our guidance takes many forms: NICE guidelines (clinical, social care, public health, medicines practice), technology appraisals, interventional procedures, medical technologies, diagnostics and highly specialised technologies.

say.text: St Thomas’ is public NHS care run by Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust. For a complaint, the official England route is trust or commissioner first, normally within 12 months, then the Public Service Ombudsman if you are still unhappy; for compensation, this is a clinical negligence claim with a usual 3-year limit, handled against the trust with NHS Resolution meeting the costs under the NHS trust scheme. Free complaint help exists through PALS and NHS complaints advocacy, and to find a solicitor you can use the Law Society’s Find a Solicitor search for Clinical Negligence in London; the trust’s own complaint and records pages were found but blocked to the agent in this run, so some trust-specific form details could not be verified.

route.summary: St Thomas’ is public NHS care run by Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust. Free complaint help exists through PALS and NHS complaints advocacy, and to find a solicitor you can use the Law Society’s Find a Solicitor search for Clinical Negligence in London; the trust’s own complaint and records pages were found but blocked to the agent in this run, so some trust-specific form details could not be verified.

sources.quote: Information supplied by Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust

Contact your local integrated care board (ICB) for complaints about primary care services (GPs, dentists, opticians or pharmacists) and secondary care, such as hospital care, mental health services, out-of-hours services, NHS 111 and community services like district nursing.

You can either complain to the NHS service provider directly (such as a GP, dentist surgery or hospital) or to the commissioner of the services, which is the body that pays for the NHS services you use. You cannot complain to both.
Complaints should normally be made within 12 months of an incident or of it coming to your attention.
At the time it acknowledges the complaint, the responsible body must offer to discuss with the complainant, at a time to be agreed with the complainant—
As soon as reasonably practicable after completing the investigation, the responsible body must send the complainant in writing a response, signed by the responsible person, which includes—

steps.body: Public Service Ombudsman
steps.what: If you are still unhappy after complaining to Guy's and St Thomas' or the commissioner first, the independent escalation route is the Public Service Ombudsman for NHS complaints in England. It uses a complaint checker which leads into the online complaint form; if you want payment as an outcome, the Ombudsman says you need to have explored legal action first and it cannot investigate where legal action was an option.
steps.deadline: "If you're still unhappy, complain to us within 12 months of knowing about the issue"
points: You must complain to the organisation first.
Complain to the Ombudsman within 12 months of knowing about the issue.
Use its complaint checker first.
The checker starts by asking what your complaint is about.
The Ombudsman says it has a three-step process.
If you want payment from the complaint route, you must first have explored legal action.
requires: If seeking payment from the complaint route, explore legal action first.
steps.appliesIf: You have already complained about NHS care in England and remain unhappy with the result or handling.
alternatives: Clinical negligence compensation claim through the courts/NHS Resolution.
Use the hospital complaint route first if you have not yet done so.
missing: Whether the trust has sent its complaint response yet.

sources.quote: Complain to the organisation you're unhappy with first
If you're still unhappy, complain to us within 12 months of knowing about the issue
Use our complaint checker to see if we can help.
To start with, please tell us what is your complaint about?
We have a three-step process for dealing with complaints.
If you are looking for payment as an outcome from your complaint then you will need to have explored the option of taking legal action before you come to us.

steps.body: NHS Resolution / Clinical Negligence Scheme for Trusts / courts of England and Wales
steps.what: For harm from NHS care at St Thomas' Hospital, compensation is by a clinical negligence claim, usually settled or litigated under the courts of England and Wales, not by a no-fault scheme. Guy's and St Thomas' remains the legal defendant, but NHS Resolution handles the claim and pays the associated costs through the Clinical Negligence Scheme for Trusts because all NHS Trusts and Foundation Trusts in England belong to it.
steps.deadline: "Compensation claims for personal injury are subject to a ‘limitation period’ of three years."
points: To get compensation, the claimant must prove both breach of duty and causation.
If acting without a lawyer, NHS Resolution says to send a 'letter of claim' to the NHS Trust responsible for the care.
Personal injury clinical negligence claims are subject to a three-year limitation period.
All NHS Trusts, including Foundation Trusts, in England currently belong to CNST.
When a claim is made, the NHS body remains the legal defendant but NHS Resolution handles the claim and meets the associated costs.
NHS Resolution also uses mediation and other dispute resolution methods to avoid unnecessary court proceedings where possible.
steps.appliesIf: You seek money for harm caused by allegedly negligent NHS treatment at St Thomas' Hospital.
alternatives: NHS complaints procedure to get explanations before or alongside considering a claim.
Mediation or other NHS Resolution dispute resolution methods during a claim.
missing: Exact date of knowledge for limitation purposes if argued later.
Whether any limitation exception could apply, such as lack of capacity.

sources.quote: To receive compensation, you will need to show both ‘breach of duty of care’ and ‘causation’ has taken place.

If you do not have legal representation and you plan on representing yourself in court as a litigant in person, you will need to submit what is called a ‘letter of claim’ to the NHS Trust that was responsible for your care.
Compensation claims for personal injury are subject to a ‘limitation period’ of three years.
Although membership of the scheme is voluntary, all NHS Trusts (including Foundation Trusts) in England currently belong to the scheme.
When a claim is made against a member of CNST, the NHS body remains the legal defendant.
However, we take over full responsibility for handling the claim and meeting the associated costs.

steps.body: Legal Aid Agency / Ministry of Justice / NHS Resolution
steps.what: For an adult clinical negligence claim like this in England, ordinary civil legal aid is generally not available. The main funding route is usually a conditional fee agreement ('no win, no fee'); for personal injury claims, the success fee taken from damages is capped by law.
points: Civil legal aid for clinical negligence remains in scope only for a neurological injury causing severe disability to a child around birth, not for a standard adult fracture-misdiagnosis claim.
The official legal aid adviser finder says advisers will ask about your problem and finances to work out eligibility.
The official search route is by postcode for clinical negligence advisers in England and Wales.
In personal injury claims, success fees are capped at 25% of specified damages and not future pecuniary loss.
The 25% cap applies at first instance.
NHS Resolution's complaints/claim pages do not offer a no-fault redress funding scheme for this kind of case.
steps.appliesIf: Clinical negligence claim in England and Wales; this patient's story is an adult NHS hospital claim.
alternatives: Conditional fee agreement with a clinical negligence solicitor.
Privately funded claim or self-representation, though NHS Resolution gives a letter-of-claim template for litigants in person.

Search for official legal aid advisers in England and Wales.
When you contact the adviser they'll ask about your problem and finances to work out if you can get legal aid.

Article 5 provides that, in a claim for personal injuries, the success fee shall be limited to a maximum of 25% of the damages awarded for pain, suffering and loss of amenity and pecuniary loss, other than future pecuniary loss and net of any sums recoverable by the Compensation Recovery Unit, inclusive of VAT.
Article 5 further limits the effect of the 25% cap to proceedings at first instance.

Advice for claimants - NHS Resolution (https://resolution.nhs.uk/services/claims-management/advice-for-claimants/)
The page says that to bring a clinical negligence claim you need to show both a breach of duty of care and causation, and if you do not have legal representation you should send a ‘letter of claim’ to the responsible NHS Trust. It says NHS Resolution handles claims for clinical negligence compensation, and it does not mention any no-fault or redress scheme on this page. The starting point it gives is that you may wish to use the NHS complaints procedure first, and it says personal injury claims are subject to a three-year limitation period, with no limitation period for people who lack capacity.
Quotes: "To receive compensation, you will need to show both ‘breach of duty of care’ and ‘causation’ has taken place." | "If you do not have legal representation and you plan on representing yourself in court as a litigant in person, you will need to submit what is called a ‘letter of claim’ to the NHS Trust that was responsible for your care." | "Before making a claim it is worth considering using the NHS complaints procedure in order to find out more about what happened." | "Compensation claims for personal injury are subject to a ‘limitation period’ of three years."

Clinical negligence services are in scope for civil legal aid only for a claim for damages for clinical negligence that caused a neurological injury to an individual who is severely disabled, and only where both conditions are met. says.text: Compensation: NHS Resolution / Clinical Negligence Scheme for Trusts / courts of England and Wales. For harm from NHS care at St Thomas' Hospital, compensation is by a clinical negligence claim, usually settled or litigated under the courts of England and Wales, not by a no-fault scheme. Guy's and St Thomas' remains the legal defendant, but NHS Resolution handles the claim and pays the associated costs through the Clinical Negligence Scheme for Trusts because all NHS Trusts and Foundation Trusts in England belong to it. (one official source)

Paying for help: Legal Aid Agency / Ministry of Justice / NHS Resolution. For an adult clinical negligence claim like this in England, ordinary civil legal aid is generally not available. The main funding route is usually a conditional fee agreement ('no win, no fee'); for personal injury claims, the success fee taken from damages is capped by law.

Clinical guidance: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). The national body that publishes the core health and care guidance used by NHS services in England is NICE. Its guidance is not a hospital complaint route, but it is the main official source to check the clinical guidance doctors are expected to use alongside specialist and local guidance. (one official source)

Free help: NHS complaints advocacy / Healthwatch / NHS PALS. Free help exists before or during an NHS complaint. NHS England says you can use PALS at most hospitals, and if you are making or thinking about making a complaint you can get free help from an NHS complaints advocate; advocates are independent of the NHS. (one official source)

Finding a lawyer: The Law Society of England and Wales. To find a clinical negligence solicitor for a St Thomas' claim, use the Law Society's official Find a Solicitor directory. It lets you search by legal issue and location, such as Clinical Negligence and London or your postcode.

trace.text: Read The Conditional Fee Agreements Order 2013: The note says that in a claim for personal injuries, the success fee is capped at 25% of certain damages. The cap applies to "the damages awarded for pain, suf…
trace.detail:
Question: What does this official legislation note say about the cap on success fees in personal injury claims and what damages the cap applies to? Quote exact wording.
The note says that in a claim for personal injuries, the success fee is capped at 25% of certain damages. The cap applies to "the damages awarded for pain, suffering and loss of amenity and pecuniary loss, other than future pecuniary loss and net of any sums recoverable by the Compensation Recovery Unit, inclusive of VAT."
✓ quote found in the page: "Article 5 provides that, in a claim for personal injuries, the success fee shall be limited to a maximum of 25% of the damages awarded for pain, suffering and loss of amenity and pecuniary loss, other than future pecuniary loss and net of any sums recoverable by the Compensation Recovery Unit, inclusive of VAT."
✓ quote found in the page: "Article 5 further limits the effect of the 25% cap to proceedings at first instance."
✓ quote found in the page: "the maximum success fee which may be recovered from damages awarded for pain, suffering and loss of amenity and pecuniary loss, other than future pecuniary loss and net of any sums recoverable by the Compensation Recovery Unit, shall be a maximum of 100% of those damages, inclusive of VAT."

trace.detail:
Question: What does this official page say about how to complain about NHS hospital care in England, who to complain to first, and the time limit? Quote exact wording and links worth following.
For NHS hospital care in England, the page says you can complain to your local integrated care board (ICB), and for secondary care it specifically includes “hospital care.” It says you can also complain directly to the NHS service provider, but “You cannot complain to both.” Complaints should normally be made within 12 months of an incident or of it coming to your attention.
✓ quote found in the page: "Contact your local integrated care board (ICB) for complaints about primary care services (GPs, dentists, opticians or pharmacists) and secondary care, such as hospital care, mental health services, out-of-hours services, NHS 111 and community services like district nursing."
✓ quote found in the page: "You can either complain to the NHS service provider directly (such as a GP, dentist surgery or hospital) or to the commissioner of the services, which is the body that pays for the NHS services you use. You cannot complain to both."
✓ quote found in the page: "Complaints should normally be made within 12 months of an incident or of it coming to your attention."

The page says the Ombudsman uses “a three-step process for dealing with complaints,” with Step 1 checking whether it can look into the complaint, Step 2 deciding whether to investigate, and Step 3 investigating if needed. It says Step 1 should be completed “within five working days,” and for Step 2 it considers factors like severity, whether something may have gone wrong, whether you complained within 12 months, and whether legal action was an option. If it investigates, the investigation has “five stages,” and “Every complaint is different so the time it takes will vary.”

Question: What does this official legislation page say about when clinical negligence services are in scope for civil legal aid? Quote exact wording that shows the rule and any limits.
Clinical negligence services are in scope for civil legal aid only for a claim for damages for clinical negligence that caused a neurological injury to an individual who is severely disabled, and only where both conditions are met. The page says the negligence must have occurred either while V was in the mother's womb or within the specified 8-week period after birth, and the services must be provided to V or, if V has died, to V's personal representative. The provision is also subject to listed exclusions.
✓ quote found in the page: "“Civil legal services provided in relation to a claim for damages in respect of clinical negligence which caused a neurological injury to an individual (“V”) as a result of which V is severely disabled, but only where the first and second conditions are met.”"

Question: What does regulation 13 say about acknowledging a complaint and discussing how it will be handled and the response period? Quote the exact wording.
Regulation 13 says that when it acknowledges the complaint, the responsible body must offer to discuss how it will be handled and the response period. The exact wording is: “At the time it acknowledges the complaint, the responsible body must offer to discuss with the complainant, at a time to be agreed with the complainant— (a) the manner in which the complaint is to be handled; and (b) the period (“the response period”) within which— (i) the investigation of the complaint is likely to be completed; and (ii) the response required by regulation 14(2) is likely to be sent to the complainant.”

Question: What does regulation 14 say about investigating a complaint and sending the response? Quote the exact wording, especially anything about times or explanations.
Regulation 14 says the responsible body must investigate the complaint "in a manner appropriate to resolve it speedily and efficiently" and keep the complainant informed "as far as reasonably practicable, as to the progress of the investigation." It must then send a written response "as soon as reasonably practicable after completing the investigation," and if it is late, it must "notify the complainant in writing accordingly and explain the reason why" and send the response "as soon as reasonably practicable after the relevant period."

Question: What does this official page say about the Clinical Negligence Scheme for Trusts, who is a member, and how it relates to clinical negligence claims? Quote exact wording.
The page says the Clinical Negligence Scheme for Trusts (CNST) "handles all clinical negligence claims against member NHS bodies" for incidents on or after 1 April 1995 (or when the body joined the scheme, if later). It says membership is voluntary, but "all NHS Trusts (including Foundation Trusts) in England currently belong to the scheme." It also says that when a claim is made against a member, "the NHS body remains the legal defendant" while NHS Resolution takes over handling the claim and associated costs.
